questions.q: Under the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), what makes accessing a protected computer a crime?
options: Lack of authorization alone — intent and whether damage occurred are not required
Only causing measurable financial damage of over a set dollar threshold
Only accessing a government-owned system specifically
Only using automated tools rather than manual techniques
questions.explain: The CFAA criminalizes unauthorized access to a protected computer regardless of intent or whether damage resulted — authorization is the determining factor, not good intentions.

questions.q: A developer tells a tester in a Slack message, "go ahead and test our app whenever." Is this sufficient authorization to begin testing?
options: Yes, any written statement from an employee of the client counts as authorization
No — real authorization is a signed contract plus a Rules of Engagement document from someone with actual authority over the systems
Yes, as long as the tester saves a screenshot of the message
No, authorization must come from a government regulator before any private engagement can begin
questions.explain: A casual message isn't authorization. A real engagement requires a signed contract and ROE, agreed to by someone who actually has legal authority over the systems in question — not just any employee.

questions.q: A client's application runs on a third-party SaaS vendor's infrastructure. The client has signed the ROE. Can the tester proceed to test that infrastructure?
options: Yes, the client's signature covers any system their application touches
Yes, as long as the vendor is mentioned anywhere in the contract
No, SaaS-hosted systems can never legally be penetration tested under any circumstances
No — testing the vendor's underlying infrastructure requires separate, explicit authorization from the vendor who actually owns it
questions.explain: Authorization only covers systems the signer actually owns. Testing a third party's infrastructure requires that third party's own explicit, written sign-off, even if the client's app runs on top of it.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the core sections a real Rules of Engagement document should contain?
options: The tester's personal home address, included for the client's records
Testing windows, including start/end dates and any blackout periods
Emergency contacts reachable throughout the testing window
An escalation procedure for critical findings discovered mid-engagement
questions.explain: A tester's personal home address has nothing to do with scope, timing, or incident handling. Real ROE sections cover testing windows, in/out-of-scope systems, permitted techniques, emergency contacts, and escalation procedures.

questions.q: A tester finds a web server that appears to already be compromised by an unrelated attacker, mid-engagement. What should happen, per a real ROE's escalation procedure?
options: The tester should quietly note it and mention it only in the final report weeks later
The tester should attempt to remove the attacker's access themselves before continuing
The tester should immediately notify the named emergency contact, rather than waiting for the final report
The tester should stop the entire engagement permanently and refund the client
questions.explain: The escalation procedure exists precisely for this scenario: critical, time-sensitive findings — like an active compromise — get reported immediately to the emergency contact, not held for the final deliverable.
